title: Canonicalization and Normalization
learning_outcomes: Explain the main security concern and trust boundary involved in Canonicalization and Normalization.
Choose an appropriate defensive control for Canonicalization and Normalization and state the assumptions under which it works.
Define a safe, reproducible verification step for Canonicalization and Normalization, including a relevant negative or failure case.

content.intro: This lesson belongs to Module 9: Input Validation, Output Encoding, and Injection Fundamentals. It builds practical understanding of Canonicalization and Normalization with the syllabus subtopics retained below.
content.why_it_matters: Canonicalization and Normalization addresses how untrusted data or requests cross a boundary and may influence application behavior. The safe fix should address the root cause and remain testable. Treat external input and identity claims as untrusted until validated, enforce the control on the server, and cover expected and denied behavior with regression tests.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Canonicalization and Normalization can be understood through this sequence: Identify input or identity → Apply server-side check → Handle failure safely → Add regression test. Start with the application asset and trust boundary, state what secure behavior should occur, and identify the evidence that would prove or disprove it.

content_blocks.title: Connect the syllabus subtopics
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum groups this lesson around: 65.1 URL encoding and decoding; 65.2 Unicode normalization considerations; 65.3 Path normalization; 65.4 Duplicate and conflicting parameters; 65.5 Consistent validation across system components. Treat these points as a checklist, not a list to memorize: explain the risk, identify the root cause, select a control, and define a test for that control.

items.title: Scope
items.text: Identify the asset, principal, input, state, or boundary affected. State whether the example is local, owned, or explicitly authorized.

items.title: Control
items.text: Treat external input and identity claims as untrusted until validated, enforce the control on the server, and cover expected and denied behavior with regression tests.

items.title: Failure behavior
items.text: Include an invalid, denied, expired, malformed, repeated, or otherwise relevant boundary case. Fail safely without exposing secrets.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Record expected versus actual behavior, a sanitized request or test result, the root cause, the chosen fix, and the regression test.

content_blocks.title: Safe reference example: Canonicalization and Normalization
content_blocks.code:
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class ContactRequest(BaseModel):
    email: str = Field(min_length=3, max_length=254)
    message: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=2000)
content_blocks.expected_output: A valid request is limited by the declared length constraints; invalid input is rejected during model validation.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Illustrative Pydantic v2 snippet. Install a compatible Pydantic version in a local environment before running it; add semantic email validation appropriate to the product.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Use a clean local test account and synthetic data. Reset the test fixture after recording the result; do not include credentials or private data in the course report.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not confuse an observation with proof or rely on a UI-only restriction. Treat external input and identity claims as untrusted until validated, enforce the control on the server, and cover expected and denied behavior with regression tests. If evidence is ambiguous, reduce the test to one condition, inspect the application code/configuration, and repeat only within the permitted scope.

content_blocks.title: Execution and safety boundary
content_blocks.text: The current CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview, not a secure runner for arbitrary server code. This example is a static reference unless the run instructions explicitly identify a supported local environment. Use a private local lab or a test system with written authorization; do not test unrelated public systems.

content.task: For “Canonicalization and Normalization”, write a short security note or test in a local/owned application. Identify the expected secure behavior, at least one relevant failure case, and the evidence needed to prove the control works.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core rule for Canonicalization and Normalization in your own words.
Name the trust boundary and the server-side control or policy that applies.
Specify a repeatable test for expected behavior and a relevant denied/failure path.
Use synthetic data and redact credentials, tokens, and personal information from evidence.
hints: Start by stating the asset, input, actor, or trust boundary and the expected secure behavior.
Change one condition at a time; record expected and actual outcomes with synthetic data.
Check the linked official reference for framework-specific settings and version-dependent behavior.
content.expected_output: A concise control explanation and a sanitized test record showing expected/actual behavior, one failure case, and a regression check.
recap: Canonicalization and Normalization is a security boundary/control topic, not a standalone checklist item.
Treat external input and identity claims as untrusted until validated, enforce the control on the server, and cover expected and denied behavior with regression tests.
Retest fixes and record sanitized evidence; use only authorized environments.
